To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of learning and savings during a visuomotor sensorimotor adaptation task can be predicted by the strength of functional connectivity in the sensorimotor, cingulo‐parietal, and default mode networks, as well as by gray matter volume in the cerebellum and the temporoparietal cortex.

the rate of visuo‐motor adaptation is related to the strength of resting‐state functional connections between the sensorimotor, cingulate, temporoparietal cortex and default mode networks and the gray matter volume of temporoparietial and occipital cortex and cerebellum.
functional and structural brain connectivity and brain volume are associated with the speed of learning and savings of a sensorimotor skill.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurophysiology of learning in the context of sensorimotor skill acquisition.
the neural predictors of sensorimotors skills.
the neural mechanisms that underlie the acquisition, consolidation, and storage of new motor skills.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cerebellum and the default mode network play a role in the storage and modification, while the temporoparietal cortex and the dorsal cingulate cortex may play a role in facilitating the cognitive aspects of adaptation.

these findings support the notion that the brain's structural and functional organization is a major determinant of individual differences in the rate of learning and memory of sensorimotor adaptations.
the cerebellum plays a key role in the acquisition of sensorimotor memories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain regions involved in early adaptation are distinct from those involved in later adaptation and savings.

the neural predictors for the rate of adaptation and multiday adaptation can be divided into two groups: one group for the early phase of adaptation (temporoparietal, cingulate) and the other group for the late phase of adaptation (default mode and cerebellum).

individual differences in the rate of sensorimotor learning are associated with differences in brain structure and functional connectivity, and the neural correlates of early and late learning may reflect the cognitive and memory components of the adaptation process, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the neural predictors of sensorimortor learning are not static but rather change over time, suggesting that the neural mechanisms of learning may be different during the early versus late phases of adaptation.
offline predictors of sensorimOTOR learning and savings are distinct, and that these predictors may be useful to inform the development of rehabilitation protocols for motor learning disorders.
the brain regions that predict offline sensorimotor adaptation and savings are not limited to the sensorimotor cortex, but also include regions that support cognitive processes and long‐term memory.
